Customer wants a short POC scoped to a 3-week pilot handling 150 reqs/s with mixed short/long prompts; security/compliance items and a latency benchmark were requested.
topics: SDK auth flows (API key, env var, SSO token exchange)
Python & TypeScript quickstart wiring and CI secrets
Sandbox vs Dedicated vs Private routing tradeoffs
Optimize playbook: batching, KV cache, quantization profiles
Security: SOC2, audit logs, KMS integration
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intro, I'm Maya AE, with Ethan our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Nair: Good thanks, excited to see how fast we can get the SDK wired in, we've got a tight timeline.
[00:11] Ethan Park: Cool, we'll try to keep this super hands-on. Today we'll show the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns, and then the Optimize playbook.
[00:20] Liam O'Connor: Quick ask — our infra team needs to understand network egress and VPC options up front.
[00:25] Maya Chen: Yep, we'll cover hosted vs dedicated vs private at a high level; Ethan will dig into VPC routing.
[00:32] -- 02:00 --
[02:00] Ethan Park: Alright, starting the demo. First step is the SDK install: pip install redwood-inference, npm i @redwood/inference — small note, package names might change, but the repo we share has exact pin.
[02:15] Sara Vega: Is there a docker image for quickly spinning local tests?
[02:18] Ethan Park: We provide a sample dev container in the quickstart repo, yes. It has env var placeholder .env.example and a docker-compose for a local runner.
[02:30] Priya Nair: Show the auth flow please — we have to avoid embedding keys in CI logs.
[02:34] Maya Chen: Totally. Two common patterns: API key via CI secret (we recommend ephemeral tokens for sandbox) and SSO-backed token exchange for Private. Ethan, walk the code.
[02:42] Ethan Park: (shares screen) In Python the snippet is basically: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY")); you can also reference a token file in the container. For TypeScript: import {RedwoodClient} from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
[03:05] Priya Nair: Any middleware for rotating keys?
[03:07] Ethan Park: We have a short helper in the repo that swaps tokens on expiry — it's not a full secrets manager. For prod we recommend hooking to your KMS/secret store and using short-lived tokens via our token-exchange endpoint.
[03:20] -- 08:00 --
[08:00] Liam O'Connor: For Private deploys, can we bring our own KMS?
[08:03] Maya Chen: Yes. Private supports customer-managed keys (HSM/KMS) and we surface integration steps in the security pack. We'll attach that doc after the call.
[08:12] Priya Nair: Great — we need SOC2 evidence too.
[08:15] Maya Chen: We'll share our SOC2 report; also show audit log samples.
[08:22] -- 12:30 --
[12:30] Ethan Park: Now the Optimize playbook. First axis: batching. We recommend continuous batching for shorter requests where latency SLO allows 50-100ms add. For Cardinal's mixed workload, a small batching window (10–20ms) could cut token cost significantly.
[12:50] Priya Nair: Our short prompts are sub-256 tokens but we have a 20% long tail at 8k tokens. How do you handle KV cache for that?
[13:00] Ethan Park: Use prefix caching and shard by user session. For long sequences we prefer a cache hit strategy: keep recent session KV to avoid recompute. Also, quantization profiles — int8 gives good perf for long-to-medium sequences.
[13:18] Sara Vega: This is the part where we worry about hallucinations — does quantization affect quality?
[13:24] Ethan Park: It can; we recommend evaluation sets. Our Optimize tool will suggest quantization per-model based on your eval pass/fail rates.
[13:35] -- 20:00 --
[20:00] Maya Chen: Let's do a quick live snippet: we'll run the Python quickstart that calls the /generate endpoint and stream tokens.
[20:10] (typing noises)
[20:25] Ethan Park: Output streaming uses SSE WebSockets in the SDK; you'll see token chunks as they arrive.
[20:35] Priya Nair: How do we measure per-token costs in our CI?
[20:38] Maya Chen: The SDK emits usage metrics client-side and our console shows token breakdown. For CI, you can call the /billing/estimate endpoint to get token cost before executing heavy jobs.
[20:50] -- 28:00 --
[28:00] Liam O'Connor: Network egress: if we run on Dedicated in us-west, do you still route through public egress?
[28:05] Ethan Park: Dedicated keeps data in your dedicated GPU pool; egress is still via region but you can use VPC peering for private deployments to avoid public transit. We'll include the network diagram.
[28:18] Priya Nair: Any rate limit behavior during bursts?
[28:21] Maya Chen: For Dedicated you can configure burst capacity and autoscaling policies. Hosted will apply soft quotas for free tiers but for paid customers we can set higher quotas.
[28:30] -- 35:00 --
[35:00] Ethan Park: Quick demo of TypeScript: we'll seed a conversation, call client.chat.create with function-calling enabled, and show a structured JSON response.
[35:12] (short pause)
[35:20] Sara Vega: We plan to use tool-calling for data lookups, will function calling be consistent across hosted and private?
[35:25] Ethan Park: Yes, same API surface. For private deployments you can disable network-facing functions or whitelist endpoints.
[35:35] Priya Nair: For our POC we need 150 req/s with 30–40% streaming responses. Can Redwood meet that on the shared hosted tier?
[35:45] Maya Chen: At those sustained rates we'd recommend Dedicated for predictability. We can do an initial hosted POC but Dedicated or a reserved capacity will give you stronger SLOs.
[36:00] -- 42:00 --
[42:00] Liam O'Connor: Cost controls — can we pin a quantization level per model per route?
[42:03] Ethan Park: Yes, per-route model config supports quantization profiles, max tokens, and batching windows. You can set fallback models for cost-sensitive routes.
[42:20] Priya Nair: Any hooks for autologging prompts for evals without storing PII?
[42:25] Maya Chen: We have masking rules and sampling options in the console; you can also opt out for certain routes.
[42:35] -- 50:00 --
[50:00] Maya Chen: Let's recap next steps: we'll share the quickstart repo, the sandbox project with a sample token, the security pack (SOC2, KMS guide), and Ethan will run the baseline latency test with their prompt set.
[50:12] Sara Vega: When can we get the baseline numbers?
[50:15] Ethan Park: Aim for results by Tuesday (2025-11-18); depends on prompt corpus size but should be quick.
[50:22] Priya Nair: We'll also send the final POC success criteria doc this week.
[50:25] Maya Chen: Perfect, once we get the criteria we can scope the Dedicated sizing if needed.
[50:32] -- 56:00 --
[56:00] Liam O'Connor: One last infra nit: can the SDK emit traces to our internal APM?
[56:04] Ethan Park: Yes, you can plug our tracing hooks to send spans to Jaeger or Datadog; we have examples in the repo.
[56:12] Maya Chen: Ok team, thanks so much. We'll follow up in email with links.
[56:20] Sara Vega: Thanks everyone.
[56:22] Priya Nair: Thanks.
[56:24] -- meeting end --
